input.subject: Better shared data structure management and resizable shared data structures

verdict_reasoning: No objection to the goal survived, and the thread shows lasting demand for online shared_buffers resizing. The surviving objections are fixable design points at level 2. The decisive ones are prior-attempts-1 (what startup reserves when huge pages are in use) and replication-ondisk-1 (protections in backends forked after a resize), which the commit message itself lists as open. Confidence is medium because only 3 of 93 messages were read directly.

brief.title: Resizable shared memory structures with reserved address space
brief.problem: Shared memory structures have a fixed size set at postmaster startup, so changing them needs a restart. The work started from resizing shared_buffers online, and the author wants a general facility for core subsystems and extensions. The thread names buffer blocks, buffer descriptors and checkpointer data as likely users.
brief.proposed_design: A structure requested with ShmemStructOpts.maximum_size gets address space for its maximum size in the main shared memory segment, which is mapped with MAP_NORESERVE, but only its initial size is backed by memory. ShmemResizeStruct() frees pages with MADV_REMOVE and allocates them with MADV_POPULATE_WRITE, so the start address never changes. The caller must coordinate access across backends, for example with a ProcSignalBarrier; optional ShmemProtectStruct() uses mprotect on the unused range.
user_visible_surface: C API: ShmemStructOpts.maximum_size and .minimum_size, ShmemResizeStruct(), ShmemProtectStruct().
pg_shmem_allocations gets new columns minimum_size, maximum_size and reserved_space; allocated_size changes meaning for resizable structures.
GUC shared_memory_size is replaced by shared_memory_initial_size, shared_memory_minimum_size and shared_memory_maximum_size.
GUC shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages is replaced by the initial, minimum and maximum _in_huge_pages variants.
New read-only GUC have_resizable_shmem (Message 73 calls it have_resizable_shared_memory) reports whether the server supports the feature.
author_claims: One mapping with madvise needs much less code than one segment per resizable structure.
Most users run Linux with mmap shared memory, so a Linux-only feature helps most of them.
Struct layout and functions are the same with or without HAVE_RESIZABLE_SHMEM, so extension builds stay ABI compatible.
Memory for future growth is not needed at startup, because the mapping uses MAP_NORESERVE.
The design is close to what a threaded server would need, so it is not a dead end (Andres Freund).
brief.thread_state: Heikki Linnakangas committed the new shmem registration API in April, and the resizable patch now sits alone in its third CommitFest. In August Palak Chaturvedi sent test portability fixes that Ashutosh partly accepted; mprotect handling, hole punching in the middle of a structure, and Windows and BSD support are still open.
unclear: The material has no numbers on the cost of MADV_POPULATE_WRITE during a resize or on extra backend startup time.
The material does not say if any core subsystem uses the feature in this patch; shared_buffers resizing is discussed in a separate thread.
The patch does not say how renaming shared_memory_size affects tools and scripts that run postgres -C shared_memory_size.
The commit message lists open items for initial protections in non-EXEC_BACKEND backends, but the excerpt is cut off.
The material does not say what happens on growth when huge pages run out, beyond a WARNING and a false return.

prior_attempts.title: Identify huge pages accessibility using madvise
prior_attempts.quote: Ah good, it looks like the issue was addressed properly in the kernel then, and we don't need the workaround your patch proposes anymore.
prior_attempts.reason: The author found that since Linux 5.7 cgroups also limit hugetlb at reservation time (hugetlb.<size>.rsvd.limit_in_bytes), so a correct setup makes the mmap fail up front. Peter Eisentraut agreed that the kernel had addressed the issue and that the workaround was no longer needed. The entry was withdrawn, and users on older kernels or with orchestration tools that do not set the rsvd limit can apply the patch themselves.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P14 probed huge page availability with madvise at startup. This proposal maps with MAP_NORESERVE, so the reservation-time check that made P14 unnecessary no longer covers the growth range.

prior_attempts.title: Detect shared buffer access violations using mprotect()
prior_attempts.quote: It'd be better to set things up so that the patch adds support for catching bad accesses with either valgrind or mprotect, according to compile options.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane asked that the patch be restructured so that bad accesses can be caught with either Valgrind or mprotect depending on compile options, using macros such as ProtectBuffer() that expand to nothing when the feature is disabled instead of inline #ifdef blocks. He also raised the concern that buffers are not reliably aligned on system page boundaries. The author did not address this feedback before the commitfest ended, so Andres Freund marked the entry returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P10 was a compile-time option that used mprotect on shared buffers to catch access-rule violations. Here ShmemProtectStruct() guards only the unused range of a resizable structure, and the thread treats it as optional.

objections.title: MAP_NORESERVE removes the huge page reservation check at startup
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA runs with huge_pages = try and sizes the hugetlb pool for shared_memory_initial_size. With MAP_NORESERVE the mmap succeeds, so there is no fallback to normal pages. Buffer blocks are not touched at startup, so a backend that first faults one of them when the pool is short gets SIGBUS, and the postmaster restarts the cluster.
objections.argument: P14 was withdrawn because the kernel charges hugetlb at reservation time, so a short pool makes mmap fail up front and huge_pages = try falls back. MAP_NORESERVE gives up that reservation for the whole mapping. Message #5 notes that unpopulated huge pages can SIGBUS, but message #7 applies MADV_POPULATE_WRITE only during resize, not at startup. The runtime.sgml hunk says the maximum huge page count must be in the pool for startup, while message #88 says only the initial memory is needed, so the proposal gives two answers.
objections.author_must_show: With huge pages, what does startup reserve or populate, and how does a short pool fail at startup without a later SIGBUS in a backend?

precedents.title: Identify huge pages accessibility using madvise

critic.reasoning: Message #5 says unpopulated huge pages can raise SIGBUS, and message #7 populates only on resize. The runtime.sgml hunk and message #88 disagree on what the pool must hold at startup.

objections.title: Per-backend mprotect state has no defined sync with postmaster and new backends
objections.failure_scenario: A subsystem grows a resizable structure and uses a ProcSignalBarrier so running backends call ShmemProtectStruct(). The postmaster does not take part in the barrier and keeps its old protections, so a backend forked afterwards inherits them. When that backend touches the newly grown range it gets SIGSEGV, and the postmaster starts a crash restart of the whole cluster.
objections.argument: The commit message in message #88 says that in non-EXEC_BACKEND builds new backends inherit stale protections from the postmaster, and lists this as an open discussion point. The proposed answer is to reapply protections next to InitLocalDataChecksumState(), which ties shmem.c to ProcSignalBarrier and adds backend startup cost. Message #73 reports that Andres sees protection as optional while Matthias wants it in shmem.c. ShmemProtectStruct() is in the series now, so the cross-process rule has to be settled before an extension relies on it.
objections.author_must_show: How does a backend forked after a resize get protections that match the current size, with no window where a barrier is missed and no help from the postmaster?

critic.reasoning: The commit message in message #88 lists initial protections in non-EXEC_BACKEND backends as an open discussion point. It proposes reapplying them at backend start but leaves the startup cost and the barrier coupling unsettled.

objections.title: API lands without a core consumer to prove its shape
objections.failure_scenario: The patch commits ShmemResizeStruct(), new pg_shmem_allocations columns and new GUCs, and the shared_buffers work then needs hole punching or a different barrier hookup at startup. Extensions that adopted the API in the meantime must change twice. Callers can change, but the view columns and GUC names are hard to take back.
objections.argument: The only user in the patch is a test module, and shared_buffers resizing is in a separate thread (message #88). Heikki asks in message #79 whether resizing only at the end is enough. In message #82 the author suggests different calls, ShmemFreeStructPart() and ShmemAllocStructPart(). The Databricks patch in message #86 makes its own coordination choices. It is not yet clear the interface fits even its first intended user.
objections.author_must_show: Can the series include, or be committed together with, a converted core subsystem such as buffer descriptors that uses this API unchanged?

critic.reasoning: Message #88 says the patch comes from the shared_buffers series, and message #82 says buffer structures resize only at the end, so a consumer exists. This entry still has only a test module as caller, so the request to commit them together stands.

objections.title: Removing shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages breaks existing scripts
objections.failure_scenario: An operator's provisioning script or an operator image runs `postgres -D $PGDATA -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages` to size vm.nr_hugepages before startup. After the upgrade the parameter no longer exists, so `postgres -C` fails. The script aborts, or it sets zero huge pages and the server falls back to normal pages. The operator finds out at deploy time, or later from lower performance.
objections.argument: The patch renames both GUCs and the matching docs, and runtime.sgml has documented `-C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages` as the way to size huge pages for years. The patch does not keep the old names as aliases and gives no deprecation period. No core subsystem uses resizable structures in this patch, so initial, minimum and maximum report the same value and users get no visible benefit yet. The old names could map to the maximum size, which is the figure the new docs tell users to provision.
objections.author_must_show: Why can shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages not stay as aliases for the maximum values, so that existing `postgres -C` users keep working?

critic.reasoning: Message #9 explains why one value no longer describes the segment, but the proposal does not say why the old names cannot stay as aliases. runtime.sgml documents `postgres -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages` today, so the break is concrete.

objections.title: Access beyond current size is silent unless each caller opts in
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch loops over a resizable array using a stale size after a shrink. Reads return zeros and writes quietly allocate pages again, so memory is not returned and the data looks valid. Nobody notices until a user sees RSS that does not shrink, or wrong results.
objections.argument: Message #3 states that a write past the current size allocates memory silently and a read returns zeros. Protection depends on each subsystem calling ShmemProtectStruct() after every resize. Andres and Matthias disagree on whether that should be optional (message #73). The commit message leaves the non-EXEC_BACKEND startup case open, so the safety net is incomplete even for callers that opt in.
objections.author_must_show: Can protection be on by default, at least in assert-enabled builds, so that a stale size fails loudly in every backend?

critic.reasoning: Message #3 confirms that reads past the current size return zeros and writes allocate silently. The thread weighed this (messages #5, #73) without agreeing, and the xfunc.sgml text leaves protection after a resize to each caller.

refuted.title: Removing shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages breaks huge page provisioning scripts
refuted.failure_scenario: A deployment tool runs `postgres -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages`, as runtime.sgml documents today, to size vm.nr_hugepages. After a major upgrade the parameter no longer exists, so the step fails or yields an empty value. Admins find out when the new cluster will not start with huge_pages = on.
refuted.argument: The patch replaces shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages with initial, minimum and maximum variants, and edits the documented huge page recipe to match. Every installation pays for this, including the many with no resizable structure. If the server has no resizable structures, all three values are equal. The material does not say why the old names cannot stay as aliases.
refuted.author_must_show: Why can shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages not stay, reporting the maximum, so that existing `postgres -C` users keep working?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the same script breakage and the alias question more fully.

refuted.title: Every resizable subsystem keeps a fixed-size path for other platforms
refuted.failure_scenario: A subsystem such as buffer descriptors becomes resizable on Linux. A later change to its resize logic breaks the fixed-size fallback that Windows, BSD, macOS and EXEC_BACKEND builds use. The failure shows up only on buildfarm animals that few developers run locally.
refuted.argument: The feature is off on Windows, EXEC_BACKEND, SysV and kernels without the MADV flags. In message #80 Andres doubts that facilities working across processes exist on all operating systems. So each converted subsystem needs two paths with no end date, and the Linux path is the one developers test. The open item on applying protections at backend start also adds per-backend startup work, and the material gives no cost figures.
refuted.author_must_show: How will a subsystem that uses resizable structures keep its non-resizable path tested, and what does backend startup cost once protections are applied there?

critic.reasoning: The fallback is the existing fixed-size code, and message #72 keeps structs and functions the same with or without HAVE_RESIZABLE_SHMEM. CFbot and the buildfarm cover the other platforms, and SysV shared memory turns the feature off on Linux for local tests.

refuted.title: Extensions get a second, Linux-only path for growable shared memory
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension author uses ShmemResizeStruct() for a growable cache because the docs present it as the way to resize shared memory. The extension then fails to request its structure on Windows, BSD, macOS or EXEC_BACKEND builds, where have_resizable_shmem is off. DSA would have worked on all of them.
refuted.argument: Postgres already lets extensions grow shared state after startup with DSM, DSA, dshash and the dsm_registry named segments, and these work on all platforms. The xfunc.sgml hunk documents resizable structures for add-ins without saying when DSA is the better choice. The fixed address is required for buffer blocks and descriptors (message #1), but most extensions do not need it. Message #80 says other platforms may never support the feature across processes.
refuted.author_must_show: Which extension use cases need a fixed-address resizable structure that DSA or dshash cannot serve, and will the docs point other extensions to DSA?

critic.reasoning: Messages #1 and #54 give the reason for a new mechanism: structures in the main segment need a stable start address, which DSA and dshash do not provide. The remaining request is a documentation pointer to DSA, which is outside levels 1-2.

refuted.title: No in-tree user of the facility ships with this patch
refuted.failure_scenario: A committer pushes ShmemResizeStruct() and ShmemProtectStruct() before any subsystem calls them. The shared_buffers resize work in the other thread may then need a different contract, such as hole punching (message #79) or other lock rules. If so, the committed API is reworked or kept for extensions that never asked for it.
refuted.argument: The demand in the material is for online shared_buffers resizing: Andres's list of buffer structures in message #1, and the Databricks internal patch in message #86. No one in the thread asks for the general facility on its own, and no extension author asks for it. The resize consumer lives in a separate thread, so this patch has no caller that shows the API fits its only real user. Message #82 also expects the API to change, to ShmemFreeStructPart()/ShmemAllocStructPart().
refuted.author_must_show: Can the shared_buffers resize patch, or another named subsystem, be committed with this API in the same release, so that a real caller exercises it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-3. As a demand objection it does not hold, because the thread shows lasting demand for shared_buffers resizing from several parties (messages #1, #86).

refuted.title: Renaming shared_memory_size GUCs costs all users for a Linux-only feature
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator's provisioning script runs `postgres -C shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages`, as runtime.sgml documents today, to size vm.nr_hugepages. After upgrading, the parameter no longer exists and the script fails or computes nothing. This affects servers where no structure is resizable and where have_resizable_shmem is off.
refuted.argument: The patch replaces shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages with initial, minimum and maximum variants for every installation. With no resizable structure registered, all three values are equal, so most users pay a compatibility cost and gain nothing. The resize benefit is limited to Linux with mmap shared memory, and in this patch only to code that registers a resizable structure. The proposal does not say why the old names cannot stay as aliases for one of the new values.
refuted.author_must_show: Why can shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages not stay, for example as the maximum value, so that existing huge-page sizing scripts keep working?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which covers the same GUC rename and the same alias question.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: pg_shmem_allocations gets minimum_size, maximum_size and reserved_space columns, and the patch edits pg_proc.dat.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: ShmemStructOpts gets maximum_size and minimum_size, and extensions can call ShmemResizeStruct() and ShmemProtectStruct().

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: Six read-only GUCs replace shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages, and have_resizable_shmem is new.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The feature works only on Linux with mmap shared memory and depends on MAP_NORESERVE, MADV_REMOVE and MADV_POPULATE_WRITE behaviour, including with huge pages.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The open item on applying protections at backend start adds work to every backend startup, and the thread gives no cost figures.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: With huge pages, what does startup reserve or populate, and how does a short pool fail at startup instead of raising SIGBUS in a backend later?
Must the huge page pool hold the maximum size at startup, as the runtime.sgml hunk says, or only the initial size, as the commit message says?
How does a backend forked after a resize get protections that match the current size, with no window where it misses a ProcSignalBarrier?
Can a converted core subsystem, such as buffer descriptors, be committed together with this API and use it unchanged?
Why can shared_memory_size and shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages not stay as aliases for the maximum values, so that existing `postgres -C` scripts keep working?

committability.owner_note: Heikki Linnakangas committed the shmem registration API this patch builds on and takes part in the thread, as does Andres Freund. The owner needs to know shmem.c, the Linux mmap and huge page code, and backend startup.
committability.liability: The owner signs for Linux-specific madvise and MAP_NORESERVE behaviour with huge pages, for a C API that extensions will adopt, and for renamed GUCs and new view columns. The names and columns are hard to change after release.
committability.author_follow_up: The author has kept the entry alive across three CommitFests, rebased it, and partly accepted test portability fixes from another contributor in August.

priority.reason: Online shared_buffers resizing has shown demand, but this patch has only a test module as caller and leaves huge page startup and backend protections open. The patch is about 129 KiB and touches shmem.c, sysv_shmem.c, backend startup and the GUC tables.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the real startup behaviour with huge pages and the placement of protection calls at backend start could not be checked. Most of the thread (90 of 93 messages) was seen only through the objections' citations.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Shared-memory based stats collector
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace the file-based stats collector with statistics kept in dynamic shared memory (dshash), so backends read stats without a stats file written by a separate process. The stats collector process goes away, and per-kind stats code moves into new files under utils/activity.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund reworked the patch in spring 2021 and judged it not committable for v14, citing weak test coverage, the need for architectural review and performance testing, an unresolved case where stats for dropped functions can be revived, and many open FIXMEs. A rebase then stalled on a new issue with partitioned tables. No new version was posted after July 2021, so the CommitFest manager marked the entry Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Unfortunately I think
that, while it has gotten a lot closer, it's still about a week's worth of
work away from being committable.

precedents_retrieved.title: NUMA shared memory interleaving
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a `numa` GUC that interleaves the shared memory segment, and later the parallel query DSM segments, across NUMA nodes with numa_interleave_memory(). Later versions add modes to restrict Postgres to a subset of nodes, for consolidation or isolation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra argued that blind interleaving ignores the internal structure of shared memory, so a buffer descriptor can land on a different node than its block, and all descriptors likely land on one node. He said later NUMA-aware work, such as per-node freelists, clocksweep and PGPROC placement, needs explicit per-structure placement and would have to largely undo this patch, and he questioned the node-subset configuration. Jakub Wartak agreed to wait for Tomas Vondra's own NUMA patch series, which was posted in a separate thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: But I just don't see how this could be 0001, followed by some later improvements. ISTM the improvements would have to largely undo 0001 first, and it would be nontrivial if an optimization needs to do that only for some part of the shared memory.

precedents_retrieved.summary: Shared Memory Context

precedents_retrieved.title: WIP: Track relation size in shared memory
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a pool of SMgrSharedRelation objects in shared memory that holds the authoritative size of each recently extended or truncated relation until the file is fsync'd, so backends stop calling lseek(SEEK_END). The aim was fewer system calls and correct sizes on filesystems such as NFS that can shrink files asynchronously; an earlier recovery-only size cache from the same thread was committed separately (c5315f4f).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stayed at prototype stage. The author said a main piece was missing: a background process to clean dirty SR objects, so that foreground processes rarely block on fsync during eviction. Review comments from Buzhen, Andres and later Anastasia Lubennikova were still open, for example on CREATE DATABASE, which bypasses smgr, and on temporary relations. The visible messages show no reply after the July 2021 review before the entry was closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The main thing being: how can we clean these objects in the background?  That question being unanswered, there is a 0% chance of committing this in PostgreSQL 14.

precedents_retrieved.title: Initial mach based shared memory support.
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a macOS-only shared memory implementation, mach_shmem.c, that calls Mach VM functions directly instead of going through the System V shared memory wrapper. The goal was to avoid the wrapper's segment limits, which caused shmget failures when a test suite started many postmasters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that Postgres uses System V shared memory mainly because it is globally visible and reports how many processes are attached. PGSharedMemoryIsInUse uses this to detect live children of a dead postmaster. The Mach mappings are task-bound, so they cannot give this interlock. David Steele found the approach needed to be reconsidered and marked the entry Returned with Feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
That is,
PGSharedMemoryIsInUse is not some minor ancillary check, it's the main
reason this module exists at all.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert recent change to RequestNamedLWLockTranche().
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert recent change to RequestNamedLWLockTranche().
Reverted commit(s): Move dynamically-allocated LWLock tranche names to shared memory.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 38b602b028 modified this function to allocate enough space
for MAX_NAMED_TRANCHES (256) requests, which is likely far more
than most clusters need.  This commit reverts that change so that
it first allocates enough space for only 16 requests and resizes
the array when necessary.  While at it, remove the check for too
many tranches from this function.  We can now rely on
InitializeLWLocks() to do that check via its calls to
LWLockNewTrancheId() for the named tranches.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Auto-tune effective_cache size to be 4x shared buffers"
Reverted commit(s): Auto-tune effective_cache size to be 4x shared buffers
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit ee1e5662d8d8330726eaef7d3110cb7add24d058, as well as
a remarkably large number of followup commits, which were mostly concerned
with the fact that the implementation didn't work terribly well.  It still
doesn't: we probably need some rather basic work in the GUC infrastructure
if we want to fully support GUCs whose default varies depending on the
value of another GUC.  Meanwhile, it also emerged that there wasn't really
consensus in favor of the definition the patch tried to implement (ie,
effective_cache_size should default to 4 times shared_buffers).  So whack
it all back to where it was.  In a followup commit, I'll do what was
recently agreed to, which is to simply change the default to a higher
value.

precedents_retrieved.title: "could not reattach to shared memory" on buildfarm member dory (design review sought)
precedents_retrieved.summary: To work around intermittent "could not reattach to shared memory" failures on Windows (seen on buildfarm member dory), the proposal was to retry child process creation end-to-end when a child fails to reattach to shared memory. Two designs were offered: a simpler one where internal_forkexec() blocks until the child signals successful reattachment (possibly behind a GUC), and a faster one where the postmaster stashes the Port structure and retry count in the BackendList entry and reaper() re-forks on a specific exit status.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The simpler design cut process-creation performance roughly fivefold, while the faster design required invasive changes to platform-independent postmaster code for every process type, and its proof of concept kept backend sockets open in the postmaster. Tom Lane judged that both approaches paid too much in performance or complexity for a problem that was not understood, noting that the visible evidence did not fit the theory of an injected thread. He proposed doing nothing until the cause on dory was better understood, and the author accepted this.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I think our best course of action at this point is to do nothing until
we have a clearer understanding of what's actually happening on dory.

precedents_retrieved.title: Detect shared buffer access violations using mprotect()
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a compile-time option (-DMPROTECT_BUFFER) that uses mprotect() to mark shared buffers read-only or read-write according to pin and content-lock state, so that violations of shared buffer access rules are caught. The patch came out of a discussion of places that modify shared buffers without holding the content lock.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane asked that the patch be restructured so that bad accesses can be caught with either Valgrind or mprotect depending on compile options, using macros such as ProtectBuffer() that expand to nothing when the feature is disabled instead of inline #ifdef blocks. He also raised the concern that buffers are not reliably aligned on system page boundaries. The author did not address this feedback before the commitfest ended, so Andres Freund marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
It'd be better to
set things up so that the patch adds support for catching bad accesses
with either valgrind or mprotect, according to compile options.

precedents_retrieved.title: drop/truncate table sucks for large values of shared buffers
precedents_retrieved.summary: Speed up DROP/TRUNCATE TABLE when shared_buffers is large by looking up each block of the relation in the buffer mapping table, instead of scanning all of shared_buffers. This path is used only when the table is smaller than a threshold (25% of shared_buffers) and shared_buffers is at least 32MB.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the approach fails badly if the caller is wrong about the relation's maximum page number (for example, kernel lseek bugs). He also noted that it does not help DROP TABLESPACE or DROP DATABASE, which also scan the whole buffer pool. Heikki Linnakangas returned it with feedback, citing the issues raised, a still-unwritten alternative (delayed cleanup during the checkpoint scan), and a preference for a structure such as a radix tree that can find all buffers for a relation or database. Tom Lane added that committing a band-aid would make more complete fixes harder to pursue.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Committing a band-aid will just make it harder to pursue real fixes.

precedents_retrieved.title: Identify huge pages accessibility using madvise
precedents_retrieved.summary: With huge_pages = try, Postgres can map huge pages with MAP_HUGETLB inside a cgroup whose hugetlb limit is too low, and the first page fault then raises SIGBUS. The patch calls madvise with MADV_POPULATE_READ (Linux 5.14+) so that this case fails at startup and Postgres falls back to normal pages.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author found that since Linux 5.7 cgroups also limit hugetlb at reservation time (hugetlb.<size>.rsvd.limit_in_bytes), so a correct setup makes the mmap fail up front. Peter Eisentraut agreed that the kernel had addressed the issue and that the workaround was no longer needed. The entry was withdrawn, and users on older kernels or with orchestration tools that do not set the rsvd limit can apply the patch themselves.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Ah good, it looks like the issue was addressed properly in the kernel
then, and we don't need the workaround your patch proposes anymore.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add missing padding from MemoryChunk struct"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add missing padding from MemoryChunk struct"
Reverted commit(s): Add missing padding from MemoryChunk struct; Use MAXALIGN() in calculations using sizeof(SlabBlock)
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit df0f4feef.  It turns out the problem which was causing
the 32-bit ARM and PPC animals to fail was due to a MAXALIGN problem in
slab.c.  This was fixed by d5ee4db0e.  The padding that was added in
df0f4feef would only do anything on machines where uint64 was not aligned
to 8 bytes.  The 32-bit machines which were failing are not in that
category, so revert this commit.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent is the same idea. P14 is the only one whose recorded reason bears on this design.

Only one objection from this angle. The new pg_shmem_allocations columns are additive, and allocated_size changes meaning only for resizable structures, which no existing structure is, so existing queries keep their results.

The proposal has no on-disk, WAL, replication or wire-protocol state. The ABI concern about HAVE_RESIZABLE_SHMEM was settled in messages #72-73, and the struct is new in this release, so backpatching does not apply.

The proposal adds only a C API for trusted server code and read-only GUCs, and no SQL-callable resize function outside the test module, so an unprivileged user gains no new action. The new pg_shmem_allocations columns keep the existing superuser and pg_read_all_stats restriction, and MADV_REMOVE returns zeroed pages, so freed contents do not leak. A later patch that exposes resizing through SQL, such as the pg_resize_shared_buffers() function in message #86, would need its own privilege review.
Not applicable: four objections raised. Heikki and Andres engaged on the design, which lowers the concern about who owns the result.

For the core use case of resizing buffer blocks and descriptors in place, no existing feature works. DSM and DSA segments do not keep one stable address in every backend, so the only objection from this angle concerns extensions.

Demand for the end goal, online shared_buffers resizing, is shown: a production patch at Databricks (message #86) and several engaged committers. The objections cover the standalone facility and the cost of the GUC rename, not the goal itself.
